messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Tax Consultant
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 52

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smoke): Smoke or fire smell, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events, Expressions of Anger: Other people expressing anger, even calmly
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event, Face Hiding: cover face with hands, Avoid Positive Events: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rajan sat in the therapist’s office with his hands pressed flat against his thighs, as if he needed to anchor himself to the chair. He was a thirty-five-year-old tax consultant, a South Asian man whose life had once been divided neatly into spreadsheets and deadlines, before he had taken a six-month leave to work as a relief coordinator in a conflict zone. That decision had dismantled him in ways he was only beginning to understand.

The event itself had not been a single explosion or a gunfight. It had been a slow, grinding horror that culminated in one afternoon he could not piece back together. He had been tasked with organizing aid distribution in a village that had been shelled the night before. The air was thick with the smell of smoke—not the clean smoke of a campfire, but the acrid, chemical burn of smoldering plastic and timber. He remembered running toward a collapsed school, remembered the heat on his face, remembered the sound of a child crying somewhere beneath the rubble. Then there was a man—a local translator named Farid—who had grabbed Rajan’s arm and pointed at a secondary building that was still intact. Rajan had hesitated. He had been trained to prioritize triage, to avoid secondary collapses. He had told Farid to wait. And then the building had exploded, not from a shell but from a gas canister. Farid had been thrown backward. Rajan could not remember the order of what happened next. He remembered his own body on the ground, his hands covering his face, the same position he had been in when the blast wave hit. He remembered the shame—the hot, crawling shame—because he had not gone into that building. He had not saved anyone. He had covered his face.

Now, back in the United States, Rajan could not tolerate the smell of smoke. A neighbor’s barbecue on a summer evening sent him into a cold sweat. He would close all the windows and sit in the dark, his hands pressed over his mouth and nose. He had stopped driving past the local cemetery because the sight of headstones made him think of Farid, of the bodies he had helped carry, of the faces he had failed to protect. He had come to believe that he was fundamentally different from other people now. They walked through their days laughing at trivial things, while he carried the weight of what he had done—or, rather, what he had not done. When a colleague at the tax firm expressed frustration about a client’s late paperwork, Rajan felt his chest tighten. Even calm anger in others felt like an accusation. He would excuse himself to the bathroom and stand there, trembling, until the feeling passed.

His wife had noticed the changes. He no longer wanted to go to social gatherings, and he actively avoided anything that might make him feel happy. A promotion at work, a kind word from a friend, a beautiful sunset—these things felt dangerous to him, as if allowing himself hope would be a betrayal of the dead. He had started working late, not out of diligence, but because he found it harder to feel safe at night. In the dark, the memories came more easily, and his body would lock into that same posture—hands over his face, knees drawn up—as if he were still lying in the rubble. Ordinary sounds made him jump: a car backfiring, a door slamming, even the ding of a microwave. He could not concentrate on his spreadsheets for more than ten minutes at a time. His manager had pulled him aside twice to ask if everything was all right.

What finally brought Rajan to therapy was the isolation. He had stopped answering his brother’s calls. He had told his wife he did not want to attend his nephew’s birthday party because there would be balloons popping and children shouting, and he knew he would startle and everyone would look at him. He had seen the hurt in her eyes, and he had felt a fresh wave of shame. He was failing to protect his own family now, just as he had failed Farid. He came to the first session because he was terrified that his marriage was slipping away, and because he was even more terrified that he deserved to lose it. He hoped, vaguely, that someone could help him make sense of the jumble in his head—to put the memories in the right order, to stop his body from reliving a moment he could not even fully remember. But what he feared most was that the therapist would confirm what he already believed: that he was broken, that he had failed, and that there was no going back.
